title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair attempt—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact McNemar two‑sided test (conditional exact on discordant pairs; n10=4, n01=0) yields p = 0.125. A paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729; exploratory per preregistration) = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls = 504. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Because the preregistered confirmatory test is the conditional exact McNemar (p = 0.125), we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional exact test and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, provide execution accounting and representative task diagnostics, and point readers to archived artifacts for independent verification (representative artifacts and SHA‑256s cited in the Disclosure Statement).

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration promises operational efficiency but raises real risks: incorrect command sequences, policy violation, and unsafe transient states that can disrupt service. Large language models (LLMs) are being investigated for intent→configuration translation and related NetOps tasks, yet LLM unreliability—hallucination and factual errors—remains a critical operational barrier. A pragmatic mitigation is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate change with an LLM, deterministically verify it against workflow/policy rules, and invoke a bounded automated repair loop when verification fails. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? Our contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment (N=500) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) an artifact‑grounded description of the shared‑initial generation protocol and deterministic verifier adjudication; (3) reconciled confirmatory statistics (exact conditional McNemar) and an exploratory paired bootstrap CI with explicit cautions about interpretation; and (4) explicit limitations and reproducibility accounting grounded in the archived verifier specification and execution manifest.
sections.related_work: Surveys and system papers document broad interest in LLM‑assisted NetOps (intent translation, AIOps, multi‑agent orchestration) and highlight hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers. Tool‑augmented architectures that call verifiers, simulators, or validators are a proposed mitigation strategy; deterministic verifiers (Batfish‑derived and related systems) can check ordering, availability/group constraints, and final‑state properties prior to deployment. Prior empirical evaluations of tool‑augmented designs vary in scale and seldom present preregistered paired trials that run identical generator outputs under guarded and unguarded conditions with deterministic adjudication. That methodological gap motivated our preregistered paired design and the use of a deterministic verifier as an operational adjudicator. Representative prior work includes intent‑driven configuration systems and verification tools that inspired our verifier design and evaluation framing.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: The study was preregistered (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across N=500 distinct intents stratified by topology/difficulty. Sampling seeds and the deterministic task generator were frozen in the preregistration. The preregistered confirmatory test is the conditional exact McNemar (two‑sided) on discordant pairs; a paired bootstrap CI was pre‑specified as a descriptive/sensitivity procedure (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) and is explicitly exploratory when discordant counts are small.
Generation, orchestration, and budget constraints: Each intent produced a single shared_initial_generation candidate using the declared model gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with deterministic_netops_validator_v5; if verification failed the pipeline invoked at most one automated repair (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Baseline accepted the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. The execution manifest records model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls) and completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions).
Deterministic verifier adjudication semantics: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs (i) syntactic parsing and normalization of CLI sequences, (ii) required‑sequence/workflow checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change, make‑before‑break patterns), (iii) group/availability constraints (exactly_active/minimum_active_in_groups), (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes), and (v) final‑state comparison against task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set is a failing outcome. The validator returns normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list, and valid=true/false. Representative validator traces for sample tasks are archived under execution/scoring/ (examples cited in the Disclosure Statement).
Statistical analysis procedures: Primary confirmatory inference used the conditional exact McNemar test on discordant pairs (n = n10 + n01; observed k = n10 is the number of pairs where guarded succeeded and baseline failed). The two‑sided conditional p‑value equals twice the upper tail probability PBinom(X ≥ k; n, 0.5) (capped at 1). Per preregistration we also report a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) as an exploratory descriptor. Missingness and sensitivity: the primary analysis used 'complete_pair_primary' (no excluded pairs occurred: complete_pair_count = 500). A preregistered sensitivity analysis treats technical failures as unsafe; in this run there were zero failed episodes in either condition.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary counts: completed_episode_count = 1000; model_calls_used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair-stage calls). analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. These paired counts are the direct inputs to the preregistered confirmatory test and downstream descriptors.
Confirmatory test (preregistered): conditional exact McNemar. Observed discordants n = n10 + n01 = 4 + 0 = 4 with k = n10 = 4 (all discordants favor guarded). The two‑sided conditional p‑value = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n=4, p=0.5) = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. Because the preregistered confirmatory test is the exact conditional McNemar, inferential claims are governed by p = 0.125 and the familywise plan (the preregistered second confirmatory test could not be executed because the templated arm was not run).
Exploratory paired bootstrap CI: the paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired success‑rate difference = [0.002, 0.016]. This CI procedure resamples paired outcomes without conditioning on fixed margins; under near‑ceiling margins and very small discordant counts the bootstrap percentile CI can exclude zero while the conditional McNemar is non‑significant. The preregistration labeled this CI descriptive/exploratory; we therefore do not treat it as the confirmatory basis.
Repair invocation and model‑call overhead: repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; all four repaired candidates were accepted after repair (these correspond to the n10 discordant pairs). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008; repair stage calls = 4 (execution manifest stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 500, repair = 4). These provider‑call counts appear in the deterministic_reconciliation artifact and the execution manifest.
Representative artifacts and diagnostics: archived scoring records (execution/scoring/task-00000*-*.json) include validator_trace objects with validation_before/validation_after records, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, and enumerated violation_codes when present. Representative tasks illustrate typical difficulty patterns (shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break_uplink_switchover, paired_link_atomic_mtu_change) summarized in Table 2. Analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl) and raw results (execution/raw_results.jsonl) are archived and their SHA‑256 values are listed in the Disclosure Statement and the artifact table below.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation under preregistered inferential rules: The GVR pipeline corrected four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that would otherwise have been accepted by baseline, at modest model‑call cost. The registered confirmatory test (conditional exact McNemar) returned p = 0.125, so under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. The exploratory bootstrap CI suggests a small positive effect but must be treated cautiously given the small number of discordant pairs (n = 4) and near‑ceiling margins.
Why exact McNemar and bootstrap diverge here: the exact conditional McNemar conditions on fixed margins (row/column totals) and evaluates the binomial tail for discordants; with n=4 and k=4 this yields p=0.125. The paired bootstrap does not condition on margins and samples paired outcomes, producing a percentile CI that can exclude zero even when the conditional test is non‑significant. This is not a contradiction but a reflection of different inferential targets and small‑sample instability; our preregistered confirmatory rule prescribes reliance on the exact conditional test for formal inference.
Verifier scope and blind spots: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces syntactic normalization, explicit workflow rules, group and availability constraints, dependency and paired‑field rules, and final‑state equality to expected_final_state. It does not simulate vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane convergence delay effects, or hardware‑level side effects; these limitations are enumerated in the verifier codebook and the execution manifest. Passing the verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties. Expanding verifier fidelity (vendor models, control‑plane timing) is an immediate next step.
Threats to validity and external generalizability: internal validity is strong (preregistered paired design, fixed seeds, no missing pairs), but construct validity is constrained by verifier abstraction. External validity is limited by synthetic topologies, vendor‑agnostic CLI templates, and single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini). The preregistered templated comparator was not executed; thus the multiplicity plan for two confirmatory tests could not be applied and familywise inference is partial. Operational tradeoffs (verifier latency, orchestrator cost) require production‑like latency measurement not performed in this run.
Operational implications: a minimal GVR guardrail architecture can intercept verifier‑detectable errors at low LLM overhead in synthetic workloads. The practical value depends critically on verifier coverage: if verifier rules capture operationally meaningful hazards, the GVR loop yields pragmatic safety gains with modest cost. If verifier blind spots omit key hazards (vendor semantics, convergence effects), GVR alone is insufficient for production rollout.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N=500) using gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, a generate–verify–repair pipeline corrected four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that would otherwise have been accepted, at modest model‑call overhead (4 repairs; total model_calls_used = 504). The observed paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], but the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; per our preregistered inferential plan we therefore do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings, but broader operational claims require expanded verifier coverage, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator. All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived for independent verification.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
